blocks.text: 1. NDCG

blocks.alt: Graded relevance produces a discounted gain, giving an NDCG score

blocks.text: Mean Reciprocal Rank closed by placing itself alongside precision and recall as three different lenses on retrieval. NDCG, a graded relevance metric that rewards a well ordered entire ranked list, combines ideas from all three into one richer score.
It scores every position with a graded relevance level, discounted by how deep it appears in the ranking.
2. Binary Relevance Versus Graded Relevance

blocks.alt: Binary relevance is compared against graded relevance on a scale

blocks.text: Precision and recall treat every chunk as either relevant or not relevant, nothing in between.
NDCG instead allows a chunk to be somewhat relevant, highly relevant, or not relevant at all.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Relevance model","Possible judgments"],"rows":[["Binary","Relevant or not relevant only"],["Graded, used by NDCG","Not relevant, somewhat relevant, highly relevant"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Discounted Gain Penalizes Deep Position

blocks.alt: A top position is compared against a deep position, which is discounted

blocks.text: A relevant chunk buried at position ten contributes less to the score than the same chunk at position one.
The discount shrinks logarithmically as position gets deeper.
4. Cumulative Gain Across The Ranked List

blocks.alt: Position 1 and position 2 accumulate into cumulative gain

blocks.text: Unlike MRR, discounted cumulative gain sums the discounted relevance across the entire ranked list.
Every relevant chunk contributes to the score, not just the first one.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A ranked list with three relevant chunks at positions one, three, and seven has all three contribute to discounted cumulative gain, unlike MRR which would only score based on the chunk at position one.

blocks.text: 5. Normalizing Against The Ideal Ordering

blocks.alt: The actual ordering is normalized against the ideal ordering

blocks.text: Raw discounted cumulative gain is not comparable across queries with different numbers of relevant chunks.
Dividing by the score of the best possible ordering normalizes it into a comparable zero to one range.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Score","What it represents"],"rows":[["Discounted cumulative gain","Raw score, not comparable across queries"],["NDCG","Normalized against the ideal ordering, comparable across queries"]]}

blocks.text: 6. NDCG Captures Both Coverage And Ordering
As with precision recall tradeoff in practice in Recall At K, precision and recall measure coverage, while MRR measures speed to one hit.
NDCG combines coverage of relevant chunks with how well they are ordered, in one score.
7. Graded Relevance Requires More Labeling Work

blocks.alt: A binary label is fast while a graded label is slower

blocks.text: As with extraction confidence scores in Entity Extraction, assigning a graded relevance level takes more labeling effort than a simple relevant or not relevant judgment.
NDCG's richer signal comes with a real evaluation cost.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Labeling each chunk as not relevant, somewhat relevant, or highly relevant, takes real human judgment time for every query in the evaluation set, a cost precision and recall's binary labels do not carry.
blocks.text: Labeling each chunk as not relevant, somewhat relevant, or highly relevant takes real human judgment time for every query in the evaluation set, a cost precision and recall's binary labels do not carry.
8. NDCG At K Combines With The Familiar Cutoff
As with the K in precision at K is a choice in Precision At K, NDCG is typically computed at a chosen cutoff, written as NDCG at K, just like precision and recall.
The same cutoff idea, applied here to a graded rather than binary metric.
9. Recognizing When NDCG Earns Its Added Labeling Cost

blocks.alt: Ordering quality mattering points toward tracking NDCG

blocks.text: A system where relevance varies by degree benefits from NDCG's graded scale.
A system where relevance is cleanly binary is served fine by precision, recall, or MRR.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates computing discounted cumulative gain, the ideal ordering, and the resulting NDCG score.

code.content:
import math

def dcg(relevance_scores):
    # discounted gain penalizes deep position
    return sum(
        score / math.log2(position + 1)
        for position, score in enumerate(relevance_scores, start=1)
    )

def ndcg(relevance_scores):
    # normalizing against the ideal ordering
    actual = dcg(relevance_scores)
    ideal = dcg(sorted(relevance_scores, reverse=True))
    return actual / ideal if ideal > 0 else 0.0

# graded relevance: 0 = not relevant, 1 = somewhat relevant, 2 = highly relevant
# binary relevance versus graded relevance
retrieved_relevance = [2, 0, 1, 0, 2]

score = ndcg(retrieved_relevance)
print("Relevance scores in retrieved order:")
print(retrieved_relevance)
print(f"\nNDCG: {score:.3f}")

ideal_order = sorted(retrieved_relevance, reverse=True)
print(f"Ideal ordering would have been: {ideal_order}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the actual ranked order scoring below one because a highly relevant chunk appeared later than it should have, exactly the ordering sensitivity as discounted gain penalizes deep position.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Treating relevance as binary when the actual data supports graded judgments.
Comparing raw discounted cumulative gain scores across queries without normalizing first.
Ignoring the real labeling cost graded relevance judgments require compared to binary ones.
Choosing NDCG for a task where relevance is already cleanly binary and simpler metrics suffice.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: NDCG is a graded relevance metric that rewards a well ordered entire ranked list.
Unlike precision and recall, NDCG allows chunks to be somewhat or highly relevant, not just binary.
A relevant chunk buried deeper in the ranking contributes less, discounted logarithmically by position.
Discounted cumulative gain sums relevance across the entire list, not just the first relevant result.
Dividing by the ideal ordering's score normalizes NDCG into a comparable zero to one range.
NDCG combines coverage of relevant chunks with how well they are ordered into one score.
Graded relevance judgments take more labeling effort than simple relevant or not relevant labels.
NDCG is typically computed at a chosen cutoff, written as NDCG at K, just like precision and recall.
